# R3 — Sinai Revisited: God Has Spoken in the Eternal, Incarnate, Now Exalted Son (1:1–2:18)

**Range read in full:** raw lines 1795–2116  
**Source:** Gareth Lee Cockerill, *The Epistle to the Hebrews* (NICNT, 2012)  
**Section:** I.A under “A Very Short History of the Disobedient People of God (1:1–4:13)”  
**Evidence class default:** attributed to Cockerill (commentary voice on Hebrews’ “pastor”)

## Claims

### C1 — Sinai-and-wilderness framing of 1:1–4:13
**Locus:** 1797  
**Quote:** "he invites his hearers to envision God's people once again gathered around Sinai (1:1-2:18) and to recall their subsequent rebellion in the wilderness (3:1-4:13). The God who spoke at Sinai has now spoken in his Son, providing the \"great salvation\" (2:3) anticipated by that earlier angel-mediated revelation"  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) 1:1–2:18 re-places hearers at Sinai: the God of Sinai’s angel-mediated word has now spoken in the Son, giving the “great salvation” (2:3) that earlier revelation anticipated; 3:1–4:13 then recalls wilderness rebellion.

### C2 — Section I.A structure: God–Son conversation; climax high priest
**Locus:** 1803  
**Quote:** "the pastor introduces God's ultimate revelation (1: 1-4) by inviting his congregation to overhear the conversation between God (1:114) and his Son (2:5-18). … These first two chapters climax in 2:17-18 with a word of encouragement that announces the main theme of Hebrews - the eternal Son is the all-sufficient High Priest."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) 1:1–2:18 is structured as divine conversation: God addresses the Son from Scripture (1:5–14); the Son answers by identifying with God’s people (2:5–18); superiority to Sinai’s angelic mediators is argued both by eternal exaltation (1:5–14) and incarnate obedience (2:5–18); climax and main theme announced at 2:17–18 (eternal Son as all-sufficient High Priest).

### C3 — Summary map of 1:1–2:18
**Locus:** 1803  
**Quote:** "In summary: the Son is the fulfillment of God's OT revelation (1:1-4). Since he is far superior to the angels through whom the Old Covenant was revealed (1:5-14), it is urgent to heed God's salvation mediated through him (2:1-4). He has procured this salvation and assumed his place of preeminence through his incarnate obedience and death (2:5-18)."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Four-step map: fulfillment (1:1–4) → angel-superiority of OT mediators (1:5–14) → urgent warning (2:1–4) → salvation procured via incarnation/death/exaltation (2:5–18).

### C4 — 1:1–4 as sermon introduction and basic premise
**Locus:** 1809  
**Quote:** "The pastor begins by announcing his basic prem ise: God's self-disclosure in his Son is the climax and fulfillment of all previous revelation. This premise lays a solid foundation both for what the pastor will say about the Son's high-priestly ministry and for his urgent exhortations to faithful endurance."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Heb 1:1–4 introduces the whole sermon: climax/fulfillment of prior revelation is the premise undergirding both high-priestly theology and endurance exhortations; 1:5–14 lets God himself attest the Son’s grandeur.

### C5 — Two “halves of a bean”: spoken-in-Son + purification/session
**Locus:** 1813  
**Quote:** "Like the two halves of a bean, the two climactic statements noted above are the seed of the pastor's theological vision: (1) God \"has spoken to us in one who is Son\" (1:1-2a); (2) \"by making purification for sins, [the Son] sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high\" (1:3). This making purification and subsequent session will be explained in terms of high priesthood."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Pastor’s theological seed is twin climaxes—Son-mediated speaking (1:1–2a) and purification-then-session (1:3)—to be unpacked as high priesthood and full disclosure of sonship; hearers are to focus on the exalted Son (8:1; 12:1–3).

### C6 — 1:1–2a: continuity with Sinai-focused OT + eschatological superiority
**Locus:** 1815  
**Quote:** "These clauses articulate the basis for any sound biblical theology by affirming the continuity between God's OT revelation with its focus on Sinai and his final revelation in Christ. At the same time they anticipate what will soon be elaborated: Christ is God's final word that fulfills and thus surpasses his previous revelation."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Opening clauses affirm continuity (same God; Sinai-centered OT; one people of God by the word) and eschatological superiority (final word that fulfills/surpasses); this double focus grounds the sufficiency of Christ for perseverance.

### C7 — “Fathers” / “us”: one people; old typological of “great salvation”
**Locus:** 1821, 1823  
**Quote:** "The same God has spoken twice: \"to the fathers\" and \"to us\" … Those who have re ceived God's revelation in the Son are the true descendants of the people of God in the OT. … the old has been shown to be typological and anticipatory of the \"great salvation\" (2:3) he has provided."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Continuity markers (“fathers”/“us”) make Son-hearers true OT descendants; diversity/fragmentation of “at various times…in various ways…of old” exposes OT incompleteness vs. “at the end of these days”; the old is typological/anticipatory of the “great salvation.”

### C8 — “At the end of these days”: prophetic fulfillment window
**Locus:** 1825  
**Quote:** "By adding \"these\" the writer of Hebrews affirms that the present time is the time of prophetic fulfillment. These \"last days\" began with Christ's session and will end with his second coming, when his \"enemies\" will be made \"a stool\" under his \"feet\" (1:13). … Revelation in the Son is the \"consummation of the ages\" (9:26)."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) LXX-style “end of days” becomes “end of these days”: present = prophetic fulfillment from session to second coming; literal emphasis falls on Christ’s coming as conclusion of prophetic-revelation days; Son-revelation = consummation of the ages (9:26).

### C9 — “Son” without article; “in” not merely “by”; radio/person analogy
**Locus:** 1827, 1829  
**Quote:** "The NRSV's \"a Son\" accurately reflects the absence of the Greek definite article. This omission emphasizes the quality of sonship. … If one likens God's word through the prophets to hearing someone over the radio, then his word in the Son is like meeting the speaker in person. … God did not speak merely \"by\" but \"in\" the prophets and preeminently \"in\" the Son."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Anarthrous “Son” stresses quality of sonship; entire OT is “through the prophets” (valid yet anticipatory); God spoke “in” prophets and preeminently “in” the Son—personally, not merely instrumentally.

### C10 — Finality of Son-revelation used two interlocking ways
**Locus:** 1831  
**Quote:** "When he urges perseverance in faith he will remind his hearers that the responsibility of those who hear God's word in the Son is much greater than that of those who received earlier revelation (see 2:1-4; 10:2631; 12:25-29). When he describes Christ's high priesthood he will contend that Christ has procured an effective salvation that exposes the typological, rather than salvific, role of the Old Covenant order (4:14-10:18)."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Son-finality drives (1) greater accountability for hearers (warning chain) and (2) Old Covenant as typological not salvific once Christ’s effective salvation is shown; final salvation both supplies grace and undergirds urgency (10:19–31).

### C11 — 1:2b–3: three relative clauses; likely pastor-composed, not borrowed hymn
**Locus:** 1833  
**Quote:** "the pastor uses three relative clauses to describe the grandeur of this \"Son\" … Some have suggested that these relative clauses with descriptive participial phrases betray the presence of a familiar hymn or confession. … It is more likely, however, that the pastor composed these lines. … these relative clauses are integral to the pastor's argument as evidenced by the way he uses the biblical quotations in vv. 5-14 to substantiate their validity"  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Against hymn-source theories for 1:2b–3: vocabulary fits Jewish Alexandrian milieu (Wisdom/Philo) but order/vocabulary differ from Phil 2 / Col 1 / 1 Tim 3:16; only unique terms “radiance” and “exact imprint”; clauses are integral and will be substantiated by 1:5–14.

### C12 — Heirship first: chiastic with session; sonship fulfilled through incarnation
**Locus:** 1835  
**Quote:** "He begins, however, with heirship, both because it is rhetorically effective and because it is determinative for the meaning of sonship. … \"Whom he made heir of all\" stands in chiastic parallel with \"he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high\" (1:3d). … the eternal Son fulfills his role as Son and Heir only through his incarnation, earthly obedience, self-offering, and exaltation. … The Son fulfills beyond all expectation the promise of universal dominion given to David's heir in Ps 2:8."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Periodic predicates begin with universal heirship (not creation first): inheritance is fruition of sonship; chiastic with session; full heirship at session, fully exercised at second coming with the faithful (1:14); high priesthood intrinsic to being Son; Ps 2:8 dominion fulfilled beyond expectation.

### C13 — Creation agent + universal heir → unique identity of God
**Locus:** 1837  
**Quote:** "Through the Son God created the temporal ages of the world and all that they contain … The attribution to the Son of both creation and ultimate sovereignty shows clearly that he is included within the unique identity of God. These functions are divine prerogatives never delegated to another."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Greek for “worlds” can mean “ages”; Son as creation agent and designated universal heir includes him in God’s unique identity—prerogatives never delegated.

### C14 — Radiance (not mere reflection) + exact imprint: distinctness and identity
**Locus:** 1841, 1843  
**Quote:** "As \"the radiance of God's glory\" the Son is the \"out shining\" of who God really is. … prohibits reduction of \"radiance\" to mere \"reflection\" (NRSV). … the Son is a perfect \"imprint\" of the \"very being\" of God. … preserve the distinctness of the Son while affirming that the finality of his revelation is based on his identity with the God he reveals."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) “Radiance” = outshining of God’s nature (not mere reflection); “exact representation” = seal/coin impress of God’s being; together preserve Son’s distinctness and identity-based finality of revelation.

### C15 — “Bearing all”: sustains and directs ages to goal via purification/session
**Locus:** 1845, 1847  
**Quote:** "The universal heir and agent of creation is also the one who sustains the universe. … The Son through whom God created the world and its ages (1:2a) does more than \"sustain\" them; he also \"bears\" or \"directs\" those ages to their God-intended goal. … The immediate context suggests that the Son accomplishes God's ultimate purposes by his making purification for sins and by his subsequent session. The broader context would add his second coming."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Present “bearing all by his powerful word” affirms sovereignty and God-Son identity; more than sustain—directs ages to goal; immediate means = purification + session (plus second coming in broader context); not abstract predestination.

### C16 — Present participles vs session: between ESV timeless and Koester-exalted-only
**Locus:** 1851, 1853  
**Quote:** "The truth lies between these extremes. The Son has been the \"radiance of God's glory\" from eternity and the one \"bearing all by his powerful word\" since creation. … What the Son has been from all eternity comes to fruition and full expression in his exaltation and session."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Against both purely timeless translations and Koester’s session-only reading of “being/bearing”: eternal/from-creation description, yet article-less participles also qualify “he sat down”—eternal identity comes to fruition at session.

### C17 — “Having made purification”: instrumental aorist; path to high-priestly session
**Locus:** 1855, 1857  
**Quote:** "\"By making purification for sins\" the Son sat down at God's right hand as High Priest of his people. \"Purification\" anticipates the description of Christ's atoning work in terms of a sacrifice that provides inner cleansing … The middle voice of \"having made\" suggests that this purification was achieved in Christ's own person … This statement is a clear allusion to this sermon's key verse - Ps 110:1. … \"He sat down\" underscores the finality of the Son's session."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Aorist “having made purification” is instrumental means of session as High Priest; middle voice → purification in his own person/self-sacrifice; climax alludes to Ps 110:1; right hand = supreme authority with subordination of receiving from God; immediate purpose of grand description is obedient attention (2:1–4).

### C18 — v. 4: “became” superior / inherited name “Son” without adoptionist split
**Locus:** 1861, 1863, 1865  
**Quote:** "through his incarnation, death, and exaltation the eternal Son became the fully adequate savior of his people. The angels have no such salvific function (see 1:14). Thus he who was superior to them as the eternal Son became superior to them in a new way at the exaltation by procuring human salvation. … it is quite appropriate … for the Father to say at the occasion of his session, \"You are my Son; today I have fathered you\" (1:5)."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Rejects unreconciled dual traditions (eternal sonship vs exaltation-adoption): eternal Son becomes superior *in a new salvific way* at exaltation; exaltation = full exercise/fruition of sonship revealed to his people, so Ps 2:7 “today” at session is apt.

### C19 — Against Schenck: personal preexistence, not figurative Wisdom
**Locus:** 1867  
**Quote:** "There is no reason, as Schenck and a few others have suggested, to reduce the description of the eternal Son to figurative status because it is derived from personifications of Wisdom in Hellenistic sources. The Son's preexistence is not merely functional but personal. … The only striking verbal echo … is the occurrence of \"radiance\" in Heb 1:3 (cf. Wis 7:26). … He uses this language to include the Son within the identity of God by affirming his role as Creator, Sovereign, and agent of redemption."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Preexistence is personal not merely functional; rejects strong Wisdom-dependence (only striking verbal echo “radiance”/Wis 7:26; Hebrews attributes creation/redemption/heirship differently from Wisdom sources); Hellenistic shared milieu language used to place Son in God’s identity.

### C20 — Angel comparison: Sinai mediators; structure of 1:5–14
**Locus:** 1883, 1885, 1887  
**Quote:** "angels were believed to have been present as intermediaries on Mount Sinai. Thus it was natural to contrast the Son who embodies God's final revelation with those angelic mediators of his earlier disclosure. … All but two of his quotations (Dent 32:43; 2 Sam 7:14) come from the Psalter (Ps 2:7; Ps 104:5; Ps 45:7-8; Ps 102:25-27; Ps 110:1). … Heb 1:5-14 falls naturally into three parts, vv. 5-6, 7-12, and 13-14."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Angels chosen as supreme comparanda (heavenly throne attendants; national governance; nature; some thought authority over world to come; Sinai intermediaries); catena almost all from Psalter (+ Deut 32:43; 2 Sam 7:14); tripartite structure 5–6 / 7–12 / 13–14 with “to which of the angels?” frames.

### C21 — Catena carefully arranged to substantiate 1:2–4; not from 4QFlor list
**Locus:** 1891  
**Quote:** "All these quotations were carefully chosen and arranged to substantiate and clarify Heb 1:2-4 and to prepare for the following argument. … Ps 2:7, quoted in v. 5, gives biblical support for the designation \"Son\" in 1:2; and Ps 110:1, already alluded to in 1:3d, provides Scriptural justification for the Son's exaltation/session. … very unlikely that he took these quotations from a traditional list such as one finds in 4QFlorilegium."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Quotation chain is authorially crafted to support prologue claims and later argument, not lifted from a florilegium like 4QFlorilegium.

### C22 — 1:5: Ps 2:7 + 2 Sam 7:14; “Son” bookends; never said to any angel
**Locus:** 1895, 1897  
**Quote:** "These combined quotations move from sonship … to fatherhood … and from fatherhood … to sonship … In the Greek text they begin and end with \"Son.\" … In him Ps 2:7 and 2 Sam 7:14 have found a fulfillment that far surpasses God's relationship to the merely human descendants of David. … The singular, \"to which of the angels?\" is significant. Occasionally the angels as a group were called \"sons of [God]. However, God never singled out an angel"  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Combined Ps 2:7 / 2 Sam 7:14 center father–son filiation with “Son” first and last in Greek; fulfillment far surpasses merely human Davidic heirs; angels may be called “sons” corporately but never singularly addressed as “You are my Son.”

### C23 — “Today I have fathered you” = exaltation/session “today”
**Locus:** 1899  
**Quote:** "vv. 3 and 4 would seem to identify this \"today\" with the exaltation/session, for it was when he \"sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high\" that the Son inherited the superior name \"Son.\" … The \"today\" of the exaltation is the \"today\" in which they are called to \"hear his voice\" (3:7, 13, 15; 4:7)."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Rejects incarnation-only, second-coming-only, or detemporalized eternal-generation readings of “today”; identifies it with exaltation/session when superior name is inherited; links to Ps 95 “today” hearing in chs. 3–4.

### C24 — 1:6: angelic worship at exaltation; Firstborn; Deut 32:43 / 4QDeut32
**Locus:** 1901, 1903, 1905, 1923, 1925  
**Quote:** "this angelic homage was rendered at the Son's exalta rather than at the incarnation or second coming. … \"Firstborn\" is an appropriate designation for the \"Son\" when he enters his inheritance at the exaltation/session. … The discovery of 4QDeut32 confirms Westcott's belief that this quotation comes from Deut 32:43 in the pastor's Greek Bible. … Hebrews follows an accurate Greek translation of the primitive Hebrew text … \"Let all the angels of God worship … the exalted Son and \"heir of all\" (1:2) is the one through whom God has accomplished this salvation. Thus the angels are invited to worship him."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Angelic worship (1:6) at exaltation entrance into salvation-“world” (cf. 2:5; 12:22–24); absolute “Firstborn” (Ps 89:27 fulfillment); quotation from Deut 32:43 / Odes via Greek Bible with Qumran support for primitive “gods/divine beings” → “angels”; pastor applies angelic worship of God to the saving exalted Son.

### C25 — 1:7 / Ps 104:4: angels temporal, malleable ministers (Sinai wind/fire)
**Locus:** 1929  
**Quote:** "he underscores their finite nature. They are created, temporal, malleable beings whom God \"makes\" and \"changes.\" … When God spoke on Sinai he was accompanied by angels and surrounded by winds and fire (Exod 19:16-18; Deut 5:22-26). As awesome as those manifestations were, they betokened the temporality of the angels in comparison to one more awesome."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Ps 104:4 presents angels as created/temporal (winds/flame of fire); Sinai theophany’s wind/fire/angels, awesome yet temporary versus the Son; “ministers” prepares 1:14.

### C26 — 1:8–9 / Ps 45:6–7: Son addressed as “God”; upright scepter; anointing exaltation
**Locus:** 1931, 1933, 1935, 1937  
**Quote:** "The God who addressed the Messiah as \"Son\" in Ps 2:7 addresses him as \"God\" in Ps 45:6-7: \"Your throne, O God, is forever and ever.\" … the scepter of the Son's kingdom is \"the scepter of uprightness\" par excellence. … Anointing with the \"oil of gladness\" is a clear reference to exaltation. … The \"companions\" … are God's people … (Heb 2:5-18) … \"You have loved righteousness and hated [lawlessness]\" … describe the Son previous to, and provide the basis for, his exaltation"  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Ps 45 ascribes deity and eternal throne to the Son; Hebrews’ word order makes uprightness the scepter par excellence of his kingdom; oil of gladness = exaltation (joy of 12:2; festivity of 12:22–24), possibly anticipating priestly consecration; companions = God’s people not angels; aorists of loving righteousness/hating lawlessness anticipate obedient death (5:7–8; 10:5–10).

### C27 — 1:10–12 / Ps 102:25–27: Creator/Judge; “roll up” creation; chiastic focus
**Locus:** 1939, 1941, 1945, 1955  
**Quote:** "This Scripture confirms and amplifies the prologue's description of the Son as Creator, Sustainer, and universal Heir. … The attribution of creation directly to the Son goes beyond the agency of v. 2 and thus underscores the inclusion of the Son within the Godhead. … he appears to have substituted \"you will roll [them] up\" for \"you will change [them].\" … \"As a covering you will roll them up\" reinforces \"whom he appointed heir of all things\" from v. 2 as well as \"bearing all to its intended end by his powerful word\" in v. 3. This affirmation lays a foundation for the final judgment and shaking of the world in 12:25-29."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Ps 102 applied seamlessly after Ps 45: Son as Lord/Creator/Judge; direct creatorship beyond agency of 1:2; textual deviations (“roll up”; repeated clothing phrase) center Son’s rolling up of creation—supports heirship/bearing-to-end and prepares 12:25–29 shaking/judgment.

### C28 — 1:13–14: Ps 110:1 climax; angels as ministering spirits, not rulers/priests
**Locus:** 1959, 1961, 1963  
**Quote:** "Just as the prologue climaxed with an allusion to Ps 110:1 in 1:3d, so this chapter climaxes with its quotation. … the pastor alone used Ps 110:4 to develop the exaltation of 110:1 in terms of priesthood. … the pastor denies the popular belief that angels ruled the nations or that they performed a heavenly priestly ministry by insisting that \"all\" of them … are \"sent\" … The Son is in charge of the nations (1:2-3) and, as the pastor will affirm, he alone is heavenly Priest."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) 1:13–14 bookends with 5–6; emphatic perfect “has he ever said?” marks Ps 110:1 as climax uniting heirship (1:2b) and session (1:3d); unique development via Ps 110:4 into priesthood; 1:14: all angels are ethereal “ministering spirits” sent for heirs of salvation—denies angelic national rule and heavenly priesthood.

### C29 — Heirs of salvation: past via Son + future inheritance; bridge to 2:1–4 and 2:5–18
**Locus:** 1965, 1967  
**Quote:** "Through him they are the heirs of the OT people of God … Through him and the fulfillment he has achieved they are \"about to inherit\" (1:14) the \"salvation\" he will bring at his return (9:28). … In 2:1-4 he must begin to exhort … In 2:5-18 he follows up this exhortation by beginning to describe the effective nature of this salvation"  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) People of God are about-to-inherit salvation through the universal Heir; past continuity and future focus; 1:5–14 prepares exhortation 2:1–4; 2:5–18 then unfolds means/efficacy of the “great salvation.”

### C30 — Warning 2:1–4: less-to-greater; “things heard”; nautical drift
**Locus:** 1973, 1975, 1977, 1979, 1981  
**Quote:** "\"On account of this it is necessary for us to give much greater attention to the things heard, lest we drift away.\" … less-to-greater argumentation was common in both rabbinic and Hellenistic circles and is fundamental to the pastor's strategy … These terms suggest a nautical metaphor: the hearers must attend to their course with diligence lest through neglect they drift away and miss their intended harbor. … Careless drifting is culpable and, if unchecked, will lead to falling \"away from the living God\" (3:12)."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) First warning applies 1:1–14: inclusive “we”; attention proportionate to Son-revelation; “things heard” = non-distant divine word anticipating Ps 95; drift = nautical neglect opposite of maturity/drawing near/running; culpable path to apostasy (3:12); social pressure and lethargy as causes (10:25; 5:11–14; 10:32–39).

### C31 — Sinai angel-mediated “word” vs “great salvation”
**Locus:** 1987, 1989, 1991, 1993  
**Quote:** "His mention of angels is a clear reference to God's definitive revelation on Mount Sinai. … God's word \"through angels\" on Mount Sinai \"encapsulates and epitomizes all pre-Son [revelation].\" It was the Sinai covenant that was fulfilled in the Son (3:6; 8:1-10:18). … This \"great salvation\" is more than a \"word\" that requires obedience and pronounces judgment. It is a provision for obedience that delivers from judgment … provided by a \"Great High Priest\" (4:14) is the main theme of Hebrews. … He wants his hearers to feel that, if possible, the judgment of those faithless to the Son is even more certain than the absolutely certain judgment of those disobedient under the OT revelation."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) “Word spoken through angels” = Sinai (angel mediation in contemporary Jewish belief), epitome of pre-Son revelation and covenant fulfilled in the Son; every transgression/disobedience received just “reward” (ironic); “great salvation” is provision (not mere demand), main theme via Great High Priest; neglect → eternal loss; certainty of judgment intensified vs OT (not a claim that wilderness judgment was less than eternal).

### C32 — Validation of the new: Lord / hearers / God + signs/wonders/Spirit
**Locus:** 1995, 1997, 1999, 2001, 2003  
**Quote:** "This salvation had its beginning by being spoken through the Lord, and it was validated for us by those who heard him, God adding his witness … by signs and wonders and various miracles and apportionments of the Holy Spirit … \"Signs and wonders\" was a set description of the great miracles by which God had delivered Israel from Egypt … affirmed not only the validity of God's word in the Son but the continuity of this word with his Sinai revelation … he makes no attempt to duplicate these events but bases his argument on their past occurrence"  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Triple validation: origin spoken through the Lord (incarnation–session as content); attested by those who heard (apostolic-type witness; “apostle” reserved for Jesus at 3:1); God co-witnesses by Exodus-like signs/wonders/miracles and Spirit apportionments; hearers’ experience assumed; no mandate either to replicate or to preclude present confirmation.

### C33 — 2:5–18 continues conversation; Ps 8 interprets Ps 110:1 invitation
**Locus:** 2021, 2023  
**Quote:** "Heb 2:5-18 completes the description of the eternal, exalted Son in 1:5-14 by showing how his incarnation and suffering were the means to his exaltation as all-sufficient Savior. … God concluded his address … with the invitation found in Ps 110:1 … In Heb 2:5-9 the pastor uses Ps 8:4-6 to explain this invitation … The Son's answer in vv. 10-13 confirms the suffering … Verses 14-18 show the relevance … With this reference to high priesthood the pastor introduces the theme of his sermon anticipated since the mention of \"purification for sins\" in 1:3."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Subsections 2:5–9 / 10–13 / 14–18; Ps 8 explains the Ps 110:1 invitation so hearers grasp Son’s answer; high priesthood (2:17–18) fulfills 1:3 purification anticipation; Pioneer (perseverance urging) and High Priest (draw near for grace) as dual titles.

### C34 — Sinai typology retained: Moses foreshadows Pioneer; Aaron typifies high priest
**Locus:** 2025  
**Quote:** "The association with Sinai is maintained by the way in which Moses foreshadows the Son in his role as Pioneer just as Aaron typifies his high priesthood."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Within Sinai-revisited frame, Moses typologically foreshadows the Pioneer role and Aaron the high priesthood (anticipating 3:1–6 and 4:14–10:18).

### C35 — 2:5–9: world to come not to angels; Ps 8 applied to Christ not generic humanity first
**Locus:** 2029, 2033, 2035, 2037  
**Quote:** "the angels, therefore, most definitively, are not the ones to whom this \"coming world\" of salvation \"has been [subjected].\" … By beginning his quotation with Ps 8:4 … the pastor intentionally injects an element of dissonance … to assert Christ's humanity. … the pastor … does not intend to make a statement about humanity in general before applying the psalm to \"Jesus\" in v. 9."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) “World to come” = exalted Son’s world (1:6), inherited salvation (1:14), entered via great salvation (2:3); deduction from 1:13–14; Ps 8 begins with humanity language to assert *Christ’s* humanity; rejects two-stage reading (fallen humanity steward first, then Jesus as representative) of 2:8c—focus is faithful people of God, not humanity as such; world never said to be “subjected” even to the faithful (they inherit/enter/receive).

### C36 — Ps 8 clauses map to incarnation / exaltation / second coming
**Locus:** 2039, 2041  
**Quote:** "\"You have made him a little lower than the angels\" … affirms the incarnation … \"with glory and honor you have crowned him\" … and \"All you have subjected under his feet\" … The second and third refer to the exaltation and the second coming, respectively. Thus they are equivalent to Ps 110:1. … by omitting Ps 8:6a and by ending the quotation before 8:7 … he asserts that absolutely \"nothing\" was left \"unsubjected to him\""  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Three key Ps 8 statements: lower than angels = incarnation; crowned = exaltation (= “Sit…”); all under feet = second coming (= enemies as footstool); omissions expand “all” to absolute subjection fitting universal Heir; “not yet see” = pending visible subjection at return.

### C37 — First naming of “Jesus”; dual perfects; continued humanity of exalted Son
**Locus:** 2043, 2045, 2047  
**Quote:** "This first use of the name \"Jesus\" opens the way for the first mention of Jesus' death: it is the incarnate \"Jesus\" who has been \"crowned\" \"on account of the suffering of death\" with divine \"glory and honor\" … \"a little lower\" [not] \"for a lit tle while lower.\" … the pastor is affirming the continued humanity of the exalted and eternal Son as the representative of the people of God."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Name “Jesus” reserved for this climactic incarnate/suffering emphasis; two perfect passives = ongoing lower-than-angels humanity and ongoing crowned status; prefers “a little lower” (not temporal-only “for a little while”); paradox of still-lower-yet-exalted = incarnation’s paradox; superiority as Savior combines eternity, assumed humanity, exaltation.

### C38 — Death as suffering/obedience; “taste death” by grace of God for all
**Locus:** 2051, 2053  
**Quote:** "Hebrews normally speaks of Christ's death under the broader category of suffering … The Son's sufficient sacrifice was not a sanitary death but a perfect, continual obedience in the face of severe opposition and suffering that culminated in his death … \"so that by the grace of God on behalf of all he might taste death\" … The pastor puts no limitation on the sacrifice of Christ, save the obedient faithfulness to which he urges his hearers. … \"taste death\" … puts emphasis on Jesus' full experience of death with its bitterness and suffering."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Death introduced as “suffering of death” (obedience amid opposition); purpose clause: God’s grace initiative; benefits available for every human being without limit except required faithfulness; sermon audience is faltering people of God; “taste death” = full bitter experience, fitting one death could not hold.

### C39 — “Fitting” suffering; Pioneer who leads many sons/daughters into glory
**Locus:** 2059, 2061, 2063, 2065, 2067  
**Quote:** "it was \"appropriate\" to the character and purposes of the sovereign God … to use suffering to equip the Savior … Christ's suffering was neither a logical necessity forced upon God nor a mere decision of his will, but an appropriate expression of the divine character. … It is as \"the Pioneer of their salvation\" that the Son brings God's children into their eternal destiny. … This description of Jesus anticipates the coming comparison with Moses (3:1-6), who led God's people toward the earthly Promised Land. … Through this suffering God established Jesus as the \"Pioneer\" completely able to save"  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) 2:10: destiny-first theology; God’s many sons/daughters destined for glory if faithful; Hebrews does not treat sonship as new birth/adoption through the Son but as bringing already-called sons/daughters to destiny; suffering “fitting” (not necessity-forced or arbitrary will); Pioneer opens way by incarnation–session (cf. Forerunner 6:20); Moses parallel anticipated; plural “sufferings” = whole human trial culminating in death; “perfect” = vocational completion.

### C40 — “To perfect”: goal, moral obedience, priestly consecration transformed
**Locus:** 2069, 2071  
**Quote:** "\"To perfect\" can be used of the attainment of a goal, of achieving moral perfection, and in the LXX, in association with consecration to priesthood. The vocational perfection of the Son as Savior incorporates and transforms all of these usages. … Through that high priesthood the faithful have present access to God's throne … There is no contradiction between Christ's eternal perfection as Son and his \"being made perfect\" in his vocation as the \"Pioneer of our salvation.\""  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Vocational perfection unites goal-attainment, obedience unto death, and priestly consecration; Pioneer vocation fulfilled only through high priesthood (2:17–18); no contradiction with eternal Sonship—perfection equips him to save (cf. Matt 28:18).

### C41 — 2:11 “from one”: God of 2:10, not generic humanity/Adam/Abraham
**Locus:** 2073, 2075, 2077, 2079  
**Quote:** "the \"one\" from whom both spring is most naturally the God described in that verse as \"the one for whom are all things and by whom are all things.\" … The Son's solidarity with God's \"sons and daughters\" is rooted in God's redemptive purpose and thus was prior to and the basis for his becoming a human being … Because God's \"sons and daughters\" were thus in need of being \"made holy,\" the Son was \"not ashamed\" to identify with them … the \"sons and daughters\" must not be ashamed of Christ before a hostile world"  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Rejects generic-humanity / Adam / Abraham / universal-Father readings of “from one”; common source is God as in 2:10, Father of Son and of people in complementary ways; sanctifier/sanctified anticipates priestly work and sin/death need; “not ashamed” brotherhood calls reciprocal unashamed loyalty.

### C42 — Son’s threefold answer (Ps 22; 2 Sam 22/Isa 8:17; Isa 8:18) to Father’s 1:5–14
**Locus:** 2081, 2083, 2085, 2087  
**Quote:** "First, in v. 12 the exalted Son's quotation of Ps 22:22 … corresponds to the Father's proclamation of the Son's divine Sonship in 1:5. Second, the Son's affirmation of his human faithfulness in v. 13a (2 Sam 22:3; Isa 8:17) complements God's declaration of the Son's divine sovereignty in 1:8-12. Third, in v. 13b (Isa 8:18) the Son accepts the Father's invitation to his right hand, given in 1:13 … As Jesus cried out in dereliction, so he now announces his triumph … \"I will put my trust in him\" gains redoubled force by its dual source in both the victorious king and the distressed prophet. … When the Son proclaims, \"I, and the children whom God has given me\" (Isa 8:18), he accepts God's invitation to sit at his right hand … on their behalf."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Dialogic structure: Ps 22:22 = brotherhood after righteous-sufferer deliverance (cross → exaltation praise in congregation); dual-source trust saying (David + Isaiah) fulfills human abandonment to God; Isa 8:18 = accepting session for God-given children (Isaiah’s remnant typology); “children” preserves Son’s uniqueness while affirming solidarity and need of training (12:4–11).

### C43 — 2:14–15: blood and flesh; destroy devil’s death-power; free from fear of death
**Locus:** 2093, 2095, 2097, 2099  
**Quote:** "he himself in like manner became a partaker with them, in order that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and set free those who by fear of death throughout their lives were subject to bondage. … He conquers through death itself … the devil had the \"power of death\" because of the sinfulness of humanity. Thus, although God's people must still die (9:27 again!), by removing their sin Christ has completely bereft the devil of his ability to intimidate them with death"  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Parallel 14–15 // 16–18: incarnation for frail “blood and flesh” (order suits blood/sin-removal); victory *through* death (not mere return to life hero myth); devil’s death-power grounded in human sin; people still die but freed from lifelong death-bondage; fear of death is acute angst rooted in judgment for sin—not an ad hoc intrusion on atonement theme.

### C44 — 2:16: takes hold of Abraham’s seed, not angels
**Locus:** 2101  
**Quote:** "By calling \"those who are about to inherit salvation\" through Christ (1:14) the \"seed of Abraham\" the pastor affirms that they are the heirs of God's promise to Abraham (see 6:12-20). The Son fulfills God's covenant faithfulness by \"taking hold of' this people of God in order to bring them into \"glory\" (2:10), just as God \"took hold\" of his people in order to bring them to the Promised Land."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Present “takes hold” = ongoing personal guidance of Abraham’s seed (promise-heirs), not angels—echoes Exodus “taking hold” toward the Land; encouragement for the disheartened.

### C45 — 2:17–18: merciful and faithful high priest; atonement; help the tested
**Locus:** 2103, 2105, 2107, 2109, 2111, 2113  
**Quote:** "it was necessary for him to be made like the brothers and sisters in every way, in order that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God, to make atonement for the sins of the people. Because he himself has suffered when he was tested, he is able to help those undergoing testing. … Here, at last, is the true and ultimate \"faithful\" priest that God promised in place of Eli's corrupt descendants (1 Sam 2:35). … his primary concern is the removal of impurity. … Christ \"cleanses the conscience from dead works to serve the living God\" (9:14)! … primary concern is with the pressures of the world that would lead his hearers to withdraw their loyalty and fall away from the faith. … \"Because he himself has suffered when he was tested\" is to be preferred to \"Because he himself was tested by what he suffered\" (NRSV)."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Full likeness “in every way” required for true priesthood (cf. 5:1); merciful-and-faithful inseparable (loyalty to God + trustworthiness to people; fruition of sonship; Exod 34:6 God; 1 Sam 2:35 promise); atonement present-tense allows once-for-all sacrifice with ongoing application; resists pure propitiation-vs-expiation split—Tabernacle/covenant purity, heart cleansing, access, and covenant-curse aspects; testing primarily social pressure to apostasy; prefers “suffered when tested” (Jesus passed; help continues).

### C46 — Section close: High Priest fulfills 1:1–4 revelation; balances warning
**Locus:** 2093, 2115  
**Quote:** "The encouragement in vv. 17-18 balances the warning of 2:1-4 and will be expanded in such passages as 4:14-16 and 10: 19-25. … God's Son with whom the pastor began in 1:1-4 fulfills his role as the ultimate revelation of God by becoming the all-sufficient High Priest described in these verses. Through his obedience despite suffering this High Priest has provided the \"great salvation\" of 2:3."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) 2:17–18 closes Sinai-revisited unit: Son’s revelation-role completed as High Priest; supplies “great salvation”; intensifies and enables response to 2:1–4; whets appetite for 4:14–10:18.
